title: DFS in Reykjavík: Find the route—one deep dive!
description: Watch how DFS explores street-map neighbors by going deep before it backtracks. This visualization turns Reykjavík’s roads into a graph and shows exactly how traversal order shapes the path.
ig_caption:
🗺️⚡ DFS Takeover in Reykjavík (Miðborg)

Depth-First Search (DFS) dives into a graph by picking one neighbor and continuing until it hits a dead end—then it backtracks. In graph-theory terms, DFS performs a traversal over nodes (intersections) and edges (street connections), producing a depth-first exploration tree that reveals how *visit order* can impact which routes are discovered first.

📍Mapped to real-ish street geometry: intersections become vertices and road segments become edges, so the algorithm’s “deep dive” behavior becomes visible as it crawls through the map’s network structure. 🌐❄️

👉 Want to see how switching to BFS or adding heuristics changes the outcome? Drop a comment with your guess, and follow for more algorithm maps!

Can your route-finding algorithm “think” like a stack? In this DFS visualization, we model Reykjavík’s road network as a graph (intersections = nodes, road segments = edges) and let Depth-First Search explore neighbors by going deep first, then backtracking. 🚦
